#4227. Review: The Legend Of Zelda: Ocarina Of Time (Switch 2) - A Stunning Remake, But Not Quite Definitive

You’re not ready for this. No matter how many trailers you’ve watched or how much pre-release footage you’ve pored over, walking out into Hyrule Field for the first time in the Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake is a revelatory experience.

It’s easy to forget how impactful Hyrule Field really was in the N64 original. While the game itself is still held in remarkably high regard, its main hub world has arguably been supplanted by later entries, particularly Breath of the Wild's enormous, immersive open world. It’s pioneering, yes, but it’s also quite small and empty when viewed through a modern lens.

The remake, with its breathtaking visuals, modernised controls, and revamped soundtrack, makes it feel new again. Standing at the entrance to Kokiri Forest and panning the camera around to soak in all of the details, I had to take a beat to stop myself being overcome by the enormity of the moment.

Making everything feel new again is really at the heart of the Switch 2 remake. I want to be clear: this is basically the same game, but Nintendo has tweaked just enough to make it feel fresh. Whether it’s the slightly different chest location for the Kokiri Sword or the Cucco hiding spots in Kakariko Village, there will always be something — however small — to give you pause.

The biggest change is the visuals. Much like Star Fox, Ocarina of Time is a staggering upgrade over the original, offering an almost overwhelming amount of detail across the board. From the small trinkets on Link’s tunic (who, by the way, is definitively 'Link' here, with no renaming options) to the way shards of broken pots stay on the ground and move underfoot, every aspect has been overhauled to take advantage of Switch 2’s power.

Yet despite the almost hyperrealistic visuals, it retains the original's spirit. There was a lot of discourse about the presentation when the remake was first properly revealed, particularly around characters’ faces. Any doubts about the approach will fade away as soon as you start playing. Everything looks right; whether it’s Link’s design or Zora's Domain, this is Ocarina of Time through and through. If you’re one of the many fans who were hoping to see the Spaceworld 2000 and Wii U tech demos properly realised, this is it and more.

The visual upgrades extend to the dungeons, of course, and it's crazy how impactful they are on your enjoyment. Inside the Deku Tree feels like a living world with realistic bark walls and copious spider webs. Likewise, the shimmering reflections and ethereal soundtrack completely transform the Water Temple. Despite minimal changes to the gameplay and structure — minor alterations to puzzles ultimately have little impact — the dungeons are a joy to explore once again.

It’s not all perfect, though. Keeping such a stunning game running at 60fps on a handheld takes some jiggery-pokery, and Nintendo's solution has resulted in a few visual blemishes. Assets in the distance — mountains and trees — look overly smooth and there’s some shimmering going on when you pan the camera around. It’s nowhere near as severe as Xenoblade Chronicles X on Switch 2, but it’s definitely something you’ll notice occasionally, particularly during handheld play.

Overall resolution takes a notable hit undocked, too, to the point where even Link himself can look a little fuzzy at times. It definitely needs mentioning, although it wasn't significantly detrimental to my experience. Keeping the game running smoothly feels like the more important priority, and Nintendo has nailed that aspect.

The audio has also been completely revamped, as well. The soundtrack, while familiar, has been reworked with new orchestral renditions, and everything from the Kokiri Forest track to the final, epic battle sounds incredible. Key cutscenes also feature voice acting, and it's some of the best I've heard from a first-party Nintendo game in quite some time. Your fairy companion Navi, whose in-game interruptions have been drastically cut down, is delightfully cheerful.

Exploring Hyrule and taking in the new visuals is made all the more satisfying thanks to the new control scheme. I’ve mentioned panning the camera around a couple of times, but it’s worth stressing that full camera control is completely new - a strange thing to highlight in 2026, but the ability to properly absorb everything this world has to offer really enhances your relationship with it. You feel so much more involved, and it helps that locations like Hyrule Castle Town have been upgraded to take advantage: no more pre-rendered backgrounds, you can now soak in all of the glorious detail.

The other major addition is the ability to jump whenever you please. Again, how quaint! Yet leaping at the press of a button gives you so much more autonomy over Link’s movements, even if it doesn’t open new routes or opportunities during your quest. You still jump at the same moments to scale platforms and solve puzzles, but doing it yourself without having to run off a ledge to trigger it is both quicker and more satisfying.

Combat feels comfortingly familiar: you lock onto your enemy and slash at them with ‘Y’, altering the direction of your swing by tilting the left analogue stick. You can hop about, perform a backwards somersault, and execute a leaping attack with either ‘X’ (the default jump button) or ‘A’, while holding and releasing ‘Y’ triggers the spin attack. It’s basically the same – why fix what isn’t broken, right?

Yet every attack now lands with such ferocity — accompanied by a searing red flash and a deafening crash — that combat feels completely overhauled. Again, old is new. Indeed, it’s so effective that it even makes Tears of the Kingdom's clashes feel comparatively tame.

Making use of your various weapons and items is also much easier than before. By holding down ‘R’, you’ll bring up an item inventory that instantly looks familiar if you’ve played TOTK or Echoes of Wisdom. Displayed in a single line, you quickly scroll left and right for your weapon of choice, whether it be a Deku Stick, a Bombchu, or the Megaton Hammer. The selection is relatively limited compared to, say, Echoes of Wisdom, so I never felt the UI was unwieldy or overwhelming; I always found what I was looking for straight away.

Meanwhile, key items like the Ocarina, masks, and Iron Boots are mapped to the D-pad. The latter is especially useful in the Water Temple, which gained its reputation as a major sticking point partly due to the need to repeatedly access the main menu to equip and unequip the boots. Tapping down on the D-pad is a lot more intuitive and makes for a breezier experience.

You can also do this for the newly-designed Lenses of Truth, which function exactly as the original Lens of Truth but have been revamped as a pair of goggles instead of a magnifying glass. It makes so much more sense!

The game is littered with similar tweaks, many of which have a noticeable quality-of-life impact. Reloading now drops you in the exact location you last saved (instead of at your house as Young Link and the Temple of Time as Adult Link). Elsewhere, the new Echo Gem, a reward from the House of Skulltula quest that replaces the Stone/Shard of Agony, shines and vibrates as you approach any Gold Skulltulas.

As for the Ocarina, you can play tunes in a variety of ways, the most basic of which is by simply pressing specific inputs via the face and shoulder buttons. Holding down ‘ZL’ brings up a menu of songs you’ve learned so far - handy for a quick reminder at any given moment.

However, you can also use the Switch 2’s built-in mic to input tunes using your own voice. Simply hum the tune you want and it’ll mostly pick it up with no fuss. You have the option to practice tunes if you wish, and it makes for a cute, if gimmicky way to use the Ocarina.

I’ve not been able to test Hori’s Electric Ocarina (and who knows where Nintendo’s official instrument is at), but I whipped out my guitar to test a few songs, and lo and behold, it actually worked. It certainly won’t be my go-to method, and chances are I’ll just stick to the buttons, but it’s neat.

I've not been able to test the Zelda Notes features during the review period, but you might find it a worthwhile addition if you're keen to create and share Ocarina songs. If you have some Zelda-themed amiibo lying about, tapping one during gameplay yields a few bonus items (arrows, recovery hearts, bombs, etc.), but thankfully nothing that could be deemed essential. All welcome additions, though.

What hasn’t been added for the remake is the Master Quest, and this is a real bummer. Available via a special GameCube release and as an unlockable in the 3DS remake, Master Quest proved an excellent way for veterans to test their skills upon completing the game. Given how closely the Switch 2 remake sticks to the core structure of the original, veterans will breeze through with minimal issues. And if you do ever get stuck, the new Threads of Time feature, which essentially documents your progress, will help you get back on track.

I died just once during the entire journey because I just got caught off-guard by an Iron Knuckle in the Spirit Temple. You can increase the difficulty slightly by altering the UI to show either minimal information or no information at all, but it’s no replacement for the changes that Master Quest could have brought. I'm hopeful that it will be added via an update, but it’s a glaring omission.

The lack of multiple save files is also disappointing. Yes, you can just create additional profiles at a system level, but the game allows you just one manual save along with several autosaves. Sometimes you just want to experience the start of the game again without impacting your main save file, so this is a shame.

The one last major addition is The Hall of Fallen Foes, and this is a cool, albeit inconsequential bonus. Accessed by sleeping in a bed after a specific campaign moment, here you can gaze upon statues based on enemies you’ve slain. It’s a lovely way to properly appreciate their updated designs, and you’re also given the opportunity to replay boss fights or even take on multiple bosses in succession. The rewards for doing so are useless, but the act of optimising your battles and beating your time is fun enough on its own.

And so, even with all that knowledge, you're really not ready for this. The visuals, the gameplay, the audio – everything has been thoughtfully upgraded to such a degree that this will completely replace the original for many. While the lack of Master Quest means it falls short of being definitive, it's still a remarkable remake, and a must-buy for Switch 2.

Ocarina of Time on Switch 2 is a stellar reimagining of the original, one that completely revamps the experience with stunning visuals, modernised gameplay, and vastly improved audio. Despite some minor blemishes, this is comfortably the most visually stunning work Nintendo has ever put out, and it’s unquestionably the best way to play one of the most seminal games of all time.

That said, it is a very safe remake. Despite lots of minor changes throughout, it’s still essentially the same game you’ve likely already played, and so you might find it offers little challenge if you’re familiar with the N64 original or 3DS remake. This makes the lack of Master Quest — or really any kind of hard mode — particularly glaring, but I’m hopeful it’ll be added in the future.

Just want to point out that I feel pretty confident that we would have possibly the same level of vitriole (maybe from the other side of the argument?) if this score had been a 10/10. It feels like every time this site or IGN releases a perfect score, they are criticized for being corporate shills, Nintendoters, lazy reviewers, etc. So, let's please be respectful and kind, take a couple breaths, and try to have some perspective. I know it can be frustrating to feel like your favorite/beloved [blank] isn't getting the appreciation or glory or credibility you feel it deserves - I was hoping for a 10 here, too! - but it doesn't have to take anything away from the enjoyment of it. I guarantee you are not alone with your love and passion for these media. But let's also try to understand that we - the people writing these reviews, included - are all individuals with subjective points-of-view. Everyone else's opinions are just as valid as your own. "It’s not all perfect, though. Keeping such a stunning game running at 60fps on a handheld takes some jiggery-pokery, and Nintendo's solution has resulted in a few visual blemishes. #4226. Where To Find All Kakariko Village Cuccos In The Ocarina Of Time Remake

Sharpen your swords and stuff some Rupees into your wallet because The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake has finally been released. In this adventure game, you play as Link, a young boy who is tasked with stopping a great evil from taking complete control of Hyrule. Throughout this journey, you'll help all types of people, both to advance the main story or just to obtain additional goodies.

One of these side quests is in Kakariko Village, which requires you to find seven missing Cuccos who have escaped their pen. The reward for your efforts is an Empty Bottle, which is something you'll definitely want to snag early on. Here is where to find all seven Cuccos so you can save yourself the headache of looking all over town for them.

When you arrive in Kakariko Village, head to the south and speak to the young red-haired woman outside the empty stable. Speak to her to learn that all her chickens have escaped, and she is requesting your assistance in wrangling them up. To do so, you'll need to locate each Cucco, approach it, and hit the interact button (A) to pick the chicken up. Then just run the bird over to the pen and throw it in with ZR.

The order you rescue the Cuccos doesn't matter.

The first Cucco can be found right outside the main entrance when you enter the village on the east side. It should be right by the tree where the Foreman is hanging around. Pick up the Cucco, run it back to the pen, and throw it in. Six more to go.

The next Cucco can be found by climbing up the stairs on the north side to reach the elevated area that looks over the rest of the village. You will find the next bird right beside the stone staircase leading up to this area.

From where you've been throwing the Cuccos into, look for a building that's under construction directly across from the pen. Among the equipment and bricks will be the next Cucco. However, don't throw this one into the pen, we're going to need it first to reach a few other Cuccos.

While holding the third Cucco, run up the large staircase leading to the raised building in the south. From there, look towards the large pile of stacked bricks with a Cucco on it. Jump off the edge of the wall and use the chicken to fly across the gap to the fourth Cucco. Throw the bird you're holding onto the ground below, then pick up the one on the bricks and put it in the pen. Keep that other bird out, as you will need it to access other areas.

The fifth Cucco can be found behind the fenced-off area in the northeast corner of town. While holding Cucco, make your way up the staircase directly in front of the windmill and jump off the edge where the fence is broken. Use the Cucco to float over the high fence to the other side. Now take both Cuccos and toss them over the fence before returning them to the pen. Do not go over the fence with them right away.

Still on the other side of the high fence, look for two ladders that lead up the eastern wall where the windmill is. Climb up the ladders to find the Cucco right in front of you. Now float down to the village with this Cucco and throw all three into the pen. One left!

You can find the seventh and final Cucco inside of a box to the left of a house with a red door. This will be right by the main square where the central tree is. Roll into the box to break it, grab the Cucco, and return the bird to the pen. Once all seven are back, speak to the woman to complete this side quest and earn yourself an Empty Bottle to use.

Dark Link is even more of an aura farmer than ever before in the Ocarina of Time remake.

#4225. Love and Deepspace 5.0 update brings together all five love interests for the first time

Love and Deepspace is getting a big update to celebrate its second anniversary, and there's a lot to dig through.

If you can believe it, Love and Deepspace is almost two-years-old, and Infold Games is celebrating the moment in a few major ways. The Throne of Eros update brings the game up to version 5.0, and it’s one for fans of all love interests.

For one, this is the first time all five of them are brought together. The update is also adding some important new features, alongside anniversary events, and more.

Throne of Eros also doubles as the new Wish Pool, which is the one that has all of the game’s love interests in a single banner. This is a limited-time affair, of course, but it’s not the only thing you should look forward to here.

There’s also the Memory Growth Bonus, another limited-time event that you can take advantage of to grow your Memories. The even bigger news is that you can target your Wishes through the Xspace Echo, which lets you select five Memories to create your own pool from. You can use this to get any Memories you might not have, of course.

On the topic of Memories, you’ll also be able to unlock new second anniversary KV Memories, as part of a Yearly Highlights Event that will let you look back on your own journey with the game over the past year.

On the story and narrative side, Throne of Eros adds two new main stories, with new branches for Xavier, and Rafayel. There’s even a narrative-specific event that will run throughout the anniversary period, through which you can earn two daily outfits for each of the five love interests.

The celebrations also extend to new anniversary content like mail, and video calls. You can purchase a Yearly Pass, and check out some new arrivals at the Lunar Shop.

Beyond the anniversary content, version 5.0 also adds a new feature to the game: Home, which essentially offers a hub to get you directly to interacting with love interests that doesn’t have to do with combat or story.

You can also expect various other quality of life updates that touch on the Journal, Phone Moments Search, Resources Quick Cleanup, and new Tete-a-Tete that should make interacting with all of them more streamlined.

While this is a special banner, you should brush up on how banners work in Love and Deepspace if you’re unfamiliar. As always, it’s never not a good idea to check our Love and Deepspace codes page for some freebies.

#4224. Death Stranding Isolations Animated Series Gets New Teaser Trailer

A new teaser trailer for Death Stranding Isolations, an upcoming animated series coming exclusively to Disney+ and Hulu next year, premiered during Kojima Productions’ 10th Anniversary Exhibition Beyond the Strand. The series was first announced last year.

Death Stranding Isolations tells an original story in the Death Stranding universe set immediately after the events of the first game. Isolations is created by Japanese animation studio E&H Production (Ninja Kamui, Bullet/Bullet, Magic Knight Rayerath) and directed by Takayuki Sano.  Death Stranding creator Hideo Kojima serves as executive producer.

Today’s teaser video provides the following story synopsis:

The Death Stranding—a catastrophic series of explosions caused when the dead crept into our world and collided with the living.

In the wake of this cataclysm, many were forced to live in absolute isolation—among them, a young girl. Although this lonely existence was forced upon her, she soon grows to prefer solitude, eschewing all opportunities for real human connection and allowing herself to be strung along by fate.

In Death Stranding, legendary game creator Hideo Kojima brought you a haunting vision of a shattered world. Now, that world expands into new frontiers with a brand-new animation series.

Under the guidance of director Takayuki Sano, world-class hand-drawn animations have been brought to life by renowned studio “E&H production” (NINJA KAMUI, BULLET/BULLET, the Magic Knight Rayearth television series).

The story is set in North America immediately after Sam—the protagonist of the game—reconnects the continent by means of the Chiral Network. However, as America is reborn from the ashes, the renewed connections that bind it together bring about new and unforeseen consequences.

In this tumultuous new landscape, there are some who walk a different path to the one chosen by Sam and his Bridges comrades: a wise old man who connects people through a method that defies all reckoning; a female soldier ensnared in a cycle of war and destruction; a boy who seethes with rage at the absurdity of his life...and of course, the girl who chose to sever all ties with the outside world...Fate has other plans for her, however, and chance encounters see her launched headfirst into a world she does not recognize.

Death Stranding Isolations is coming to Disney+ and Hulu in 2027. It’s one of the three planned big-screen adaptations of the series. An animated movie called Death Stranding: Mosquito (working title) is also in the works alongside a live-action Death Stranding film by A24.

For more on Death Stranding, check out our reviews for the first game and its 2025 sequel. You can also read the latest update on Kojima Productions’ upcoming stealth-espionage game, Physint.

#4223. Genshin Impact Version Luna 4 introduces three new playable characters, including the long-awaited Moon Maiden Columbina

The first major Genshin Impact update in 2026 is almost here, bringing characters we've been waiting a while to play, and more besides.

Genshin Impact’s latest Special Program has spilled all the beans on the game’s next major update, Luna 4. The update, which arrives on January 14, kicks off 2026 with several bits of new content, including some previously-teased characters.

Dubbed Traveler on a Winter's Night, Luna 4 introduces three new playable characters, and brings back The Lantern Rite event to celebrate the beginning of the new year.

The first new arrival in Version Luna 4 is Columbina Hyposelenia, the Moon Maiden. Columbina is a 5-Star Hydro Catalyst wielder. Her kit revolves around supporting the squad via Lunar Reactions. She can trigger coordinated Lunar Reaction DMG, even when she’s off the field.

The Moon Maiden’s special ability, Lunar Domain, further boosts all Lunar Reactions by applying a DMG bonus, including summoning more thundercloud strikes for Lunar-Charged reactions. Columbina is also capable of converting Electro-Charged, Bloom, and Hydro Crystallize reactions into Lunar Reactions, as well as revive fallen squad members.

Speaking of elemental reactions, new in this version is Lunar-Crystallize, a new reaction that’s triggered when Geo meets Hydro (under certain conditions). When triggered, Lunar-Crystallize summons three Moondrifts near enemies. When triggered three times, Moondrift Harmony gets activated, dealing Geo DMG to enemies caught in its radius.

Then there’s Zibai, an Adeptus from Liyue. Zibai is another 5-Star character, a Geo Sword wielder. Zibai can, through entering a special state where they can build up energy, unleash an Elemental Skill that deals Lunar-Crystallize DMG.

The longer the fight goes on, the more Lunar-Crystallize reactions are triggered, the higher (and more often) the damage of Zibai’s Elemental Skill becomes.

Luna 4 continues the Nod-Krai story arc, with a big confrontation with Il Dottore. This is the focus of the new Archon Quest, completing which will earn you a new outfit. There’s a gameplay element to that new chapter, too, with the reveal of Piramida, a new area north of the region. Piramida is the headquarters of the Lightkeepers.

The first phase of Luna 4’s Event Wishes will, unsurprisingly, feature Columbina. It’ll also include reruns of Ineffa. The second phase is when Zibai becomes available, alongside another newcomer: Illuga, a 4-Star, polearm-wielding Geo Lightkeeper. The second phase’s rerun will be Neuvillette, who’s also going to have a new outfit in the shop at a discount.

Version Luna 4 brings back the annual Lantern Rite event, taking place in the mainland of Liyue. The event features its own set of minigames with unique rewards, alongside new stories of the Adepti.

All around Liyue Harbor, you’ll be able to place Xiao Lanterns and inscribe them with messages for others to read. You’ll also earn some Fortune Coins from Auspicious Treasure Trees, which you can later exchange for gifts.

All players will receive 1,600 Primogems through the in-game mail. If you log in regularly, you can earn up to ten Intertwined Fates. Lantern Rite has a new outfit for Yaoyao, which is also where you have a chance to earn one 4-Star Liyue character for free.

Finally, you can look forward to the new Classic Mode in Miliastra Wonderland, which lets you invite select Teyvat characters to join you.

#4222. EA Reportedly Closed BioWare To Invest In Developing Star Wars Battlefront III Instead Of The Next Mass Effect

Electronic Arts shut down the legendary RPG studio BioWare last week, ending development on an untitled fifth Mass Effect game. Since then, we've seen what appears to be a leaked trailer for the game, which suggests it might have been called Mass Effect Universe, and heard a sneak peek at what Grammy-winning composer Austin Wintory was cooking up for the beloved sci-fi RPG series. Over the past week, fans across the internet have tried to piece together how a publisher could decide to shut down a studio as prolific as BioWare, but according to a new Bloomberg report, the answer is Star Wars.

More specifically, Bloomberg writes that, presented with the opportunity to develop Star Wars Battlefront III with Disney, the publisher, which went private last year after a $55 billion acquisition,  chose to invest its money into that instead of BioWare's in-development Mass Effect sequel. The publication writes that EA looked at its portfolio for the coming years and had two massive sci-fi investments it could continue: Star Wars Battlefront III or BioWare's next Mass Effect. Even though Mass Effect was well into development, and even though the Battlefront threequel hasn't even entered development, EA chose to continue with the latter. And so BioWare was shut down, and Mass Effect development ended, though Bloomberg's sources say there are other, less significant reasons the studio was shuttered, too.

Those other factors include the poor reception to 2017's Mass Effect: Andromeda, the failure of Anthem in 2019, and 2024's Dragon Age: The Veilguard, which, despite garnering positive critical reception, apparently missed EA's sales expectations by 50%.

There's also the uncomfortable reality that BioWare made progressive LGBTQIA+ positive games but was a studio within a publisher house now partially owned by the Public Investment Fund of Saudi Arabia, a government fund from a country where same-sex activity, including marriage, is criminalized, sometimes punishable by death; these harsh laws extend to other facets of the LGBTQIA+ community. Another investment partner in this acquisition of EA is Affinity Partners, a Miami-based investment firm founded and run by former White House senior advisor Jared Kushner, who is the son-in-law of President Donald Trump, a political figure who imposes laws that discriminate against the LGBTQIA+ community, especially the 1% of Americans who are transgender; Trump has also been known to mock this community in various ways. No official statements say BioWare shut down because of its progressive leanings, but one has to wonder if that was a factor, especially after reports that BioWare scrubbed diversity from demos to avoid negative feedback from EA (thanks, Kotaku).

When BioWare closed last week, only 50 employees remained, all working on the next Mass Effect, after years of layoffs at the studio.

A Mass Effect TV series is still in the works at Amazon, even though EA seems to have hung up Commander Shepard's video game suit for good.

#4221. OG Xbox Game 'Godzilla: Destroy All Monsters Melee' Gets Remastered, But What Do The Critics Think?

Was it worth digging the original Xbox title back up?

Godzilla: Destroy All Monsters Melee launched on the original Xbox in 2003, a few months after its GameCube debut, and sadly, only in North America. The kaiju arena-brawler, which depicted the iconic King of Monsters, Godzilla, body-slamming Ghidorah into various cityscapes, has apparently made a big enough impact to warrant Atari funding a remaster in 2026.

Sadly, the whole North American release made it quite difficult for us Brits to get our mucky mitts on the game, and DAMM wasn't a big enough deal for Xbox to share the game with the rest of the world. DAMM did get the backward compatibility treatment, however, only on Xbox 360, and again restricted to North America.

I guess then, we're quite pleased Atari decided to take a punt on a DAMM remaster. Even though it seems to share many of the original's downfalls, Godzilla's WWE antics are going to be available on November 3rd on Xbox Series X|S, and best of all, I can play it from my lovely little home in Cornwall.

So, here's what the critics are saying about Godzilla: Destroy All Monsters Melee Remastered:

"Godzilla: Destroy All Monsters Melee Remastered brings the classic kaiju brawler roaring back with impressive rebuilt visuals, satisfying arena destruction, and chaotic multiplayer battles. While its limited roster and tedious character unlocks feel dated, the accessible combat and faithful Godzilla presentation make this a thoroughly entertaining return for the King of the Monsters."

"Godzilla: Destroy All Monsters Melee Remastered feels like a new game with its graphical upgrade, held back slightly by a lack of any other meaningful new additions and a somewhat grindy gameplay loop."

"Destroy All Monsters Melee Remastered is a satisfyingly faithful update to a beloved Kaiju brawler. It’s simple and fun, with local and online multiplayer keeping you around for the long haul despite a wafer-thin single-player experience. Now if we could just get a remaster of Save The Earth and Unleashed."

Review Godzilla: Destroy All Monsters Melee Remastered (Switch 2) - The King Returns With A Fun But Thin Kaiju Brawler

"Godzilla: Destroy All Monsters Melee Remastered is at its best when it simulates the idea of smashing kaiju toys together as a kid in short sessions with friends, and at its worst when it attempts to prolong a game that never had much depth to begin with. The result is a remaster I’m glad exists considering the drought of Godzilla brawlers, but with a few caveats–not to mention the sting of realizing that the original GameCube and Xbox game were absent of arbitrary grinding."

"Godzilla: Destroy All Monsters Melee Remastered remains goofy fun, and Atari’s remaster looks and runs well. It’s still a rather simple game and probably not the most comprehensive when it comes to the characters and lore. But it’s a good time and offers quite a few different modes to get acclimated and beat up famous faces."

"Right now, Godzilla: Destroy All Monsters Melee Remastered is a great version of a good retro game. Because the game was remade from the ground up, I wish the developers had made a super version of the Godzilla trilogy with more content. While Godzilla: Destroy All Monsters Melee Remastered’s combat is really fun, there’s not much depth. There are lots of modes, and a bit of RPG unlocking, but this isn’t a deep fighting game that’s going to be played at tournaments. It’s a great budget buy for Godzilla fans. But more content would have made Godzilla: Destroy All Monsters Melee Remastered a more obvious recommendation. If you’re at all curious, or have any fondness for the original game, it remains a fun time."

"In the media shadow of sacred monsters like Grand Theft Auto VI and The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time Remake, only an equally fearless monstrosity could face them: Godzilla. Nearly a quarter century after its release on GameCube, Godzilla: Destroy All Monsters Melee returns with a remaster that discreetly refreshes the audiovisual experience and improves the progression without betraying its structure. The core is that of a 3D fighting game in which kaiju clashes are accompanied by the destruction of entire cities, in a blaze of explosions and particle effects. Behind this chaos lies a combat system that's immediate, but not always precise and balanced, suspended somewhere between classic fighting games and the festive jumble of a party game. The mechanics are simple, despite a certain unwieldiness in the movements, and the best of the action is found especially in local multiplayer."

Well, there you have it, folks! Godzilla: Destroy All Monsters Melee Remastered is an almost perfect example of a good '7' rated game. At the time of writing, the remaster is holding down a 72 score on Metacritic.

What's interesting is that the original Xbox release scored 73 on Metacritic - a single point higher than the remaster. It's funny how 23 years can pass and a game can be reviewed almost identically.

#4220. Heartopia captures the hearts of Animal Crossing and The Sims fans to become the No.1 free download across 50 countries

Heartopia is officially the first big mobile launch of 2026, as the game grabs the attention of millions worldwide.

Heartopia, the new cosy life sim from XD Games, has officially arrived on mobile, right on schedule. If you’ve been keeping up with Heartopia news, you’re likely already aware that the game has pushed back its Steam release to an indeterminate point in 2026.

Doesn’t look like it mattered much, however, as this has already been a big launch on iOS and Android — it probably helps that PC players aren't being entirely left out of the fun, since the game is already available there via XD's own cross-device platform TapTap.

XD Games announced today that Heartopia has reached the top spot on the App Store’s downloads page for free games, and it managed to do so in more than 50 countries and regions worldwide.

The developer is celebratig by offering players a lot of free stuff. If you're feeling lucky, you’ll find new outfits and furniture in three gacha banners (Gilded Acorn Exhibitions): Polar Hymn, The Frostguard, and Coolplayism.

XD Games says you can expect regular updates to add more content, through Fashionwaves and Festivals. In fact, the first season - Winter Frost - is already penciled in for sometime in late January, and it’s going to add appropriately wintery activities like ice skating and snowman-building.

In February, a My Little Pony collaboration event will kick off, bringing new inspired outfits, and vehicles to the game.

Heartopia is a clever mix of Animal Crossing, and The Sims. It’s a free-to-play life sim where you can create your own character, dress them up, build a home for them (and decorate it), and go about town visiting and playing with other players’ characters.

The game’s main feature is the ability to take on a hobby, and seven of those are available at launch. You can dig deep into each hobby, either alone or with others, and there’s a progression track dedicated to each one.

Whether you’re among the millions who downloaded the game already, or you intend to so soon, we’ve got a set of helpful guides to get you started. You should check out how to unlock and upgrade hobbies in Heartopia first, before you get deep into finding all cooking recipes. And, of course, this wouldn’t be a big game launch without a bunch of Heartopia codes for some free stuff.

#4219. Diablo 4's long-awaited Tower and its Leaderboards enter beta today, and there's no PTR funny business this time

Diablo 4's first big moment of 2026 is nearly upon us, and it's one feature many have been looking forward to for actual years.

Diablo 4 is about to deliver on Blizzard’s years-old promise to add a challenging, leaderboard-driven experience to the action RPG. The beta for The Tower, and its associated Leaderboards are about to kick off.

As recently revealed, the new experience launches today at 11am PT, 2pm ET, 7pm GMT. This is a beta version that arrives alongside update 2.5.2.

This early launch won’t offer the full experience, and it’s mainly designed to get it into the hands of players early so that Blizzard could get as much feedback as possible and incorporate it into the final version.

The beta is available to everyone, which is a nice change from the usual rigmarole players would have to go through to get the PTR build and play on a different branch. The Tower, and Leaderboards will be available only in the Seasonal Realm, however. Indeed, the plan is to build on what’s there with each future season, so it’s best to think of it as a seasonal experience.

The Tower is about as simple of an activity as you can get in an action RPG. The goal is to climb as many floors as you can as quickly as you can, all while battling increasingly difficult mobs.

You need to reach and beat the Tower’s final boss before you can call it a run. The Leaderboard will then show your time, and let you see how well you did compared to other players.

The Tower is available to anyone who completed Rank 2 of the current Season Rank. Once done, an Obelisk will appear in Cerrigar, letting you access the challenge.

The Leaderboards themselves will operate on a two-week schedule, all of which will take place during a given season. In this case, they’re going to close the day before Season of the Divine Interversion - the game’s current season - ends.

Blizzard published an updated set of patch notes that show how much has changed since The Tower, and Leaderboards first became playable in the patch 2.5.0 PTR.

Though the two new additions have been anticipated for a while, there’s not been much exciting going on in the world of Diablo 4, apart, of course, from the surprise arrival of The Paladin class, which became available in December last year to coincide with the announcement of Lord of Hatred, the game’s next expansion.

#4218. How To Unlock Epona In The Ocarina Of Time Remake

The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake has officially launched, so get ready to save Hyrule once again from the evil King of the Gerudo, Ganondorf. Throughout this journey, you will encounter quite a few allies, but one of the most important is your horse, Epona.

However, unlocking this mount is completely optional, and it can be easy to miss out on acquiring her if you don't explore. Here is everything you need to know about unlocking Epona so you can easily get around Hyrule Fields without any issues.

The first step of this quest is to earn Epona's Song from Malon. This can only be done as Young Link, so make sure you're in the past if you've progressed further into the game. Once you're in the past, make your way to Lon Lon Ranch, which can be found in the middle of Hyrule Fields.

When you arrive, make sure it's daytime; otherwise, you'll need to wait or play the Sun Song to change the time of day. Go to the main corral where all the horses are to find Malon singing next to Epona. Approach and speak to her to learn that she has a song that soothes the animals at the ranch. Once your conversation is over, pull out your Ocarina while standing next to Malon.

This will prompt her to teach you Epona's Song, which you'll need later as Adult Link. This is all you have to do in the past, so don't worry about coming back here until Link is grown up.

And nearly 850 times the size of the original.

Now just progress through the story until you acquire the Master Sword and Link is an adult. Once you're free to explore Hyrule, make your way back to Lon Lon Ranch. Don't worry about the sages or any of the temples; this can be done the moment you leave Hyrule Castle Town after seeing what Ganondorf has done to the place.

When you get to Lon Lon Ranch, you'll find that Talon is missing, Malon is now relegated to working in the stables, and Ingo has taken control thanks to Ganondorf. You can talk to Malon if you want, but to get Epona you'll want to actually speak with Ingo, who is standing outside the corral. He will ask if you want to ride the horses inside, which requires you to fork over 20 Rupees. Pay him and go into the corral.

Instead of just picking any random horse, take out your ocarina and play Epona's Song. There won't be a correct audio cue if it worked, but Epona will run up to you. When this happens, climb onto her and practice riding her around the corral. You can practice riding her as much as you want and even have some small fences to practice jumping over.

Take note of the carrot icons at the bottom of your screen when riding. There will be six of them, and you can use these to give Epona a short burst of speed by pressing the A button. They will refill over time, so don't worry about overusing them or running out. When you're ready to progress, ride Epona over to Ingo and speak to him while on Epona.

Ingo will then challenge Link to a race for 20 Rupees since Epona has a history of knocking her riders to the ground. Agree to the race, which will be just a single lap around the corral. This first race is quite easy, as Ingo will assume you're going to lose and won't really seem to try.

That being said, you can still lose if you don't use the speed boost mechanic. The trick is to not use all of Epona's carrots at once. Use two near the start and first turn, two during the straightaway, and the last two when you round the final corner towards the finish line. Once you beat Ingo, he will throw a fit and ask you to race again. If you win, Epona will be all yours.

Agree to the second race, but be ready, as Ingo will both race ahead right before he gives the signal to go and will be faster this time. The catch to beating him is to be ahead of Ingo during the straight after the first turn. He gains a ton of momentum here, so this is where you want to use around three carrots to stay ahead of him. Always make sure to have a carrot for the last turn right before the finish line, as this will help you secure the win and ensure Ingo cannot catch up.

Ingo will not take losing lightly and, in a desperate attempt, he will cose the gates to trap you. Ride Epona back several meters and use your carrots to gain a lot of speed. Charge the gate head on, allowing you to jump clear of Ingo, triggering a cutscene as you escape with Epona. Congratulations! You have earned your trusty steed, which can be summoned at any time in Hyrule fields by playing Epona's Song on the ocarina.

#4217. The Top 10 Best Horror Games To Play This Halloween

Humans are drawn to horror in all forms, real life and fiction. Perhaps it’s the desire to get as close to death as possible without actually dying; perhaps it’s the morality of life and knowing death comes for all of us; perhaps all our heads are just a little miswired. Whatever the reason, we flock to movies where supernatural entities and puppets on tricycles upend otherwise lovely lives, TV shows where murderous cults kill and stump local detectives, and books where the words on the page seem to follow you to bed. Games, however, go a step further, letting you enter the horror and control it (or become its victim), and you could argue that, as a result, they’re the most immersive form of fiction.

We at Game Informer love a healthy dose of horror from time to time, and we often review games like this. Some terrify us. Others… don’t. And the best ones stick with us for years and years after the credits. Below is a list of 10 of the best horror games we’ve played recently. This isn’t an all-time list, so don’t fret if your personal favorite isn’t here. Instead, this is a collection of 10 horror games ordered by release date that we think are great for spooky season and beyond. Let us know in the comments what you would add to the list!

The cozy corner of the horror genre seems to have exploded overnight, and now tons of new slice-of-life horror games are in various stages of development. That said, the team behind newcomer The Village in the Shade is no stranger to the form; they made the Yomawari series, a cute-and-terrifying collection of creepy virtual tales. The Village in the Shade takes things back to the homestead, giving you (a child who emerged from a hole in the ground and was immediately given the responsibility of running an entire farm by yourself) the freedom to plant, sow, reap, ranch, and more. Just follow the important rules: don't go out at night, don't share secrets, and don't leave the village among others. You wouldn't want to break the rules, right? You could, theoretically, go about your idyllic rural living. But as you unravel the threads of what this village is, who you are, and why you're here, it's hard not to get drawn into the strange, mysterious, delightfully disturbing truths hiding in its shadows. Just don't forget to water your turnips before you go sneaking out again.

Fans of survival horror and old-school FMV adventure games will find plenty to love (and fear) in Tenebris Somnia. When a young woman visits her ex-boyfriend’s apartment and discovers he's trapped in a hellish dream world, it kicks off a well-executed survival-horror trek of inventive puzzles and resource management to overcome dangerous monsters. High-production, live-action cutscenes help tell the story of a deteriorating relationship and the toll an indie horror film took on its creators, and they play an important role in gameplay. Tenebris Somnia may not look like much due to its classic pixelated presentation, but its scares and story captivate. – Our Review

Resident Evil Requiem is not just one of the best Resident Evil games, but it’s also one of the best horror games ever made. It features a unique dual-protagonist structure. Grace Ashcroft is timid, new to the whole “shooting zombies in the head while dealing with Umbrella viruses” thing, and is generally just trying to do her job. Leon S. Kennedy, however, is a veteran of all that and more. Requiem splits its runtime between the two characters, letting you experience both sides of Capcom’s marquee survival-horror style. Grace’s sections leave your hands clammy and your blood pressure high as you desperately try to survive. Leon’s sections leave your hands shaking with adrenaline and your blood pumping with excitement as he mows down zombies (sometimes literally, courtesy of those pesky chainsaws). The result is a Resident Evil game that blends two typical RE experiences – terrifying and tough or exhilarating over-the-top action – into one cohesive package. It’s perfect for someone who wants to feel scared and then soon after receive the catharsis of being the one in control, like being the tragic victim who dies in Act One of the horror movie and the last one standing who lives to tell the tale. – Our Review

Little Nightmares developer Tarsier Studios has a knack for delivering creepy side-scrolling adventures, but Reanimal eschews any whimsy to become its scariest game yet. While mechanically it is similar to Little Nightmares and still puts small children in unimaginable peril, Reanimal is capital-H horror thanks largely to its terrifying threats and disturbing animal-themed imagery (this probably isn’t the game for animal lovers; some messed-up stuff happens to these critters). Escaping the game’s island setting is thrilling and chilling whether you’re playing alone or with a friend in co-op. Months after release, we’re still thinking about Reanimal’s memorable final sequence, which is worth the price of admission on its own. – Our Review

2001’s Silent Hill 2 is considered one of the best horror video games of all time for good reason. At release, it was a graphical powerhouse, using the PlayStation 2's horsepower to create a setting that begged to be explored, even though every bone in your body said you shouldn’t. The remake from developer Bloober Team took on a big task in modernizing the game without losing the original’s soul, and it did a great job. Among all the recent Silent Hill releases (Silent Hill f, Silent Hill: Townfall), the remake is our favorite. The story of James Sunderland and his troubling relationship with his departed wife is complex, emotional, and – important for the purposes of this list – unsettling and scary. – Our Review

Alan Wake 2 is an excellent pick for some spooky madness, in the vein of David Lynch’s seminal Twin Peaks mystery-surrealist series. Don’t worry too much about the “2” part of the game’s title. You just need to know that the titular Alan Wake character is a not-great writer who acts like he’s really great, his wife is missing, and he got trapped in the ambiguous Dark Place. He’s only one half of the Alan Wake 2 equation, with his segments set in a dream-like version of New York City. Playing as him feels the most Twin Peaks-y. The other half is Saga, a police officer who arrives in the Pacific Northwest town of Bright Falls to investigate a murder that might be linked to a cult. You can expect more traditional survival-horror gameplay from her. But this is still a Remedy Entertainment game, and without spoiling anything, it goes places. And along the way, you can expect plenty of scares. Turn the lights down low (or off), light a candle, and sit back and enjoy one of Remedy’s best games. – Our Review

Square Enix has gone two-for-two with its Paranormasight series, an anthology of stories about the strange and occult. And while the more recent Mermaid's Curse is a brilliant tale all its own, the first entry – The Seven Mysteries of Honjo – brings significantly more scares. A group of people in the city of Honjo find themselves caught in a spectral battle royale, using powerful objects and conditions to curse one another, with the allure of a prize at the end. Its magic isn't just in the flowchart timeline, where you can hop between different perspectives and protagonists to see how events play out from every angle, but also in the gorgeous stereoscopic environments and narrative puzzles. Adventure games are a classic genre, and Paranormasight will remind you of what the genre is capable of the moment you slowly spin your camera around, your eyes peeking out from behind your fingers.

Survival horror can contain multitudes, and as the years have worn on, the genre has grown to encompass a wide range of action-combat mechanics. Signalis feels like a re-centering in that respect. It's an isometric survival-horror indie project from developer rose-engine, filled with clever puzzles, scarce resources, limited inventory slots, and looming, oppressive dread. As the Replika unit Elster, you delve deep into a remote complex filled with horrors and monsters, searching for something, or someone, waiting down below. While love for classic horror games and other hallmarks of genre fiction will certainly draw you in, the stylish presentation and devastatingly human core will keep you forging ahead to the finale. Once you've breached the surface of Signalis' retro-future super-structures, you won't be able to turn back.

In horror movies, audiences often groan at a protagonist for putting themselves in seemingly grave danger just to learn more about a cursed amulet or bloodthirsty killer. But in Immortality, you are the protagonist, and despite a lingering sense that you shouldn't be digging into the archives of these abandoned films, each eerie new scene makes you want to dive deeper. It's a game about Marisa Marcel, an actress who almost starred in three movies in the late 20th century, but has since disappeared. None of the movies were ever released due to mysterious circumstances, but you have access to the archived, unedited live-action footage, including behind-the-scenes conversations. By scrubbing through footage, you can select people or items in each scene and jump to random footage from any other movie that includes the same person or item. The approach to puzzle-solving is unique and keeps you appropriately disoriented. The mystery at the center is an unsettling treat to unravel, and scary in new and unexpected ways. Immortality is one of a kind and an easy recommendation for horror fans who want to try something a little different.

In the decade since launch, Dead by Daylight has continued to succeed, thanks to a dedicated (and newcomer-friendly) fanbase and its towering roster of original and licensed personas from across pop culture horror. The asymmetrical multiplayer title has become an anthology of horror’s biggest faces, including Freddy Krueger, Ghostface, Pyramid Head, and even the Xenomorph. Whether you play as a Survivor, trying to escape all manner of nightmare locations through stealth and cunning, or as a Killer, whose experience feels more like a hunting club, you’ll understand why Dead by Daylight has become a recurring destination for fans of the gruesome and bizarre.

Read about the making of Dead by Daylight and how it sunk its teeth into millions of players in our six-page exclusive feature in Issue 368 (p. 42), available in our magazine archive to anyone with a free Game Informer account.

#4216. The Sims developer vows "our values are unchanged," as it teases multiple projects from post-Saudi-owned EA

The team behind one of EA's most diverse franchises has issued a statement about its future under the soon-to-be Saudi-owned publisher.

In their (slightly belated) new years message to players, the developer of EA’s The Sims series of games has lightly addressed concerns about its future within the publisher in a wide-ranging letter to the community.

The letter also serves as something of a light plan for what players can expect soon, and in the future, alongside what the various teams are currently working on.

The developer starts off the yearly check-in with a statement that attempts to address concerns about the future of The Sims, historically one of EA’s most inclusive and culturally diverse franchises.

This, of course, comes in the wake of last year’s bombshell that EA is being taken private by a coalition led by Saudi Arabia’s Public Investment Fund (PIF), alongside investment firms Silver Lake Capital and Affinity Partners. The $55 billion acquisition was approved by EA’s shareholders in December, and is set to close by the end of June.

Understandably, many raised concerns about what EA’s new ownership would mean for its people, and portfolio of games. The news is concerning for The Sims in particular, a series that’s long embraced diversity and inclusivity, and has historically been popular among women, people of colour, and members of the LGBTQ+ community.

“Our Sims team's creative control, guided by our values of inclusivity, choice, creativity, community, and play, has not changed,” the post reads, though without referring to the buyout directly at any point.

“These values inspire the decisions we make each and every day as we plan for today, tomorrow, and the future.”

As for what’s to come in 2026 and beyond, it sounds like The Sims team has multiple irons in the fire. The developer is working on “a family of new Sims experiences” that will find homes on PC, console, and mobile. Crucially, the post says that not every experience will be on every platform, in order for each to focus on delivering something different and interesting.

Future releases, of course, include new The Sims 4 content that focuses on the single-player experience. The social and more multiplayer-driven experiences, however, will instead be found in Project Rene, the mobile-first life-sim currently in development. (Despite early confidence that it was a working title for The Sims 5, it's now confirmed that Project Rene won’t, in fact, be a direct successor to The Sims 4.)

Some of these projects will see more playtesting throughout 2026, so you should probably sign up for The Sims Labs if you want to hear about when/how you can get involved.

#4215. 'Too Big A Risk' - Game Developer Sparks Debate After Delaying Playtest Due To AI Concerns

Will it push us towards a more cloud-focused future?

As AI continues to adopt a bigger influence in the gaming industry, there have been concerns in some circles about how people can use AI to reverse-engineer games, including for upcoming titles that haven't even been released yet.

This became a particular talking point a couple of weeks ago when Moonlighter developer Digital Sun Games decided to delay a planned (PC) playtest for their upcoming game ReVamp, worrying that the code might be reverse-engineered before they actually had a chance to release the full game.

Here's what they had to say in a statement at the time:

This ended up sparking a whole bunch of discussion regarding developers that might choose to adopt the same strategy, potentially opening us up to a future where demos and trials for upcoming games will become less prominent.

Some even took it further, suggesting that reverse-engineering will push us to a cloud-focused future:

A few people pushed back in the comments, suggesting that games have still been successful despite the existence of piracy and other elements that have threatened their potential over the years, while others highlighted that stronger protections in the future may be able to limit the damage from reverse-engineering situations.

For what it's worth, it's been reported in recent days that Claude has begun blocking attempts to clone and reverse-engineer games, and it was confirmed by an Anthropic dev that the idea is to "steer it away" from recreating other developers' titles because infringing IP is against the company's usage policy.

Ultimately though, it's too early to know what the future holds, but it's an interesting topic of discussion at the very least. Don't be surprised if instances like this still crop up, and hopefully it's something that Xbox is actively thinking about.

#4214. Nintendo Joins The Accessible Games Initiative, Adopting A Bunch Of New eShop Game Tags

Nintendo has joined the Accessible Games Initiative and, in the process, has added a collection of new accessibility tags to the eShop.

The new tags — which include various accessibility features like 'Narrated Menus', 'Full Input Remapping', and 'Playable with Buttons Only' — make it easier to sort through games based on specific requirements. Simply select a tag from the eShop Tags page, and it will bring up every game where that requirement can be applied.

A product of the Entertainment Software Association, the initiative has also been adopted by Amazon Games, EA, Google, Xbox, Riot Games and Ubisoft. "Our goal is to improve players’ gameplay experiences by providing clear information about the accessibility features available in video games," the Accessible Games Initiative website reads.

Here is a full list of all the tags included in the project. You can find detailed descriptions of what each of them entails on the AGI site.

The eShop is intimidating enough as it is, so we always welcome new ways of sorting through its many, many titles to find a game that suits.

What do you make of these new eShop tags? Let us know in the comments.

#4213. The Sims 4 gets a bunch of free items inspired by Coach that you can use right now

As part of a free update, The Sims 4 has kicked off a new collaboration with Coach, which means there's free stuff for everyone.

The Sims 4’s first update of the year is here, though it may not be quite what you might have expected. The game’s latest patch mainly centres around a collaboration with Coach, the luxury fashion brand.

This obviously isn’t the game’s first collaboration with a known brand, though this one does include a lot of free items and accessories that anyone can make use of, even if they don’t care about Coach.

The Coach Collection brings nine new items to The Sims 4. They range from clothes and accessories you can use with Create a Sim, to decoration items available in Build Buy. There’s also The Carriage House, a new Gallery household where you can find three new roommates.

There’s a nice bit of variety in the options available, some casual and others more practical for your Sims to wear. Then there’s The Bag Room, which can also be grabbed from the Gallery. The room simply serves as a way for you to show off your Coach bags and trunks collection.

In case you missed it, The Sims’ development team recently shared an update on some of what we can expect in 2026, both for The Sims 4 as well as other projects currently in the works. It even included further confirmation, if any was needed, that Project Rene is a dedicated mobile off-shoot, and not — as many had long believed — The Sims 5.

The blog post also included a statement about EA’s imminent change of ownership, which many fear could alter the series’ inclusive and diverse nature, and the decisions made by its various teams.

#4212. Metal Gear Solid 4: Guns Of The Patriots: Part 7 – Big Mama Mia | Super Replay

In 2008, Kojima Productions released what was billed as the swan song for Hideo Kojima's Metal Gear series: Metal Gear Solid 4: Guns of the Patriots. The game had the staggering task of tying up decades of storytelling by bringing together Solid Snake, Ocelot, Otacon, Raiden, and many more characters for one explosive finale. The adventure centers on a rapidly aging Solid Snake racing against the clock to stop his twin and nemesis, Liquid Snake, one last time. Of course, there are far more bizarre shenanigans at play.

Guns of the Patriots was acclaimed for its storytelling, cinematic presentation, and evolution of the series' stealth gameplay, namely the OctoCamo suit that allowed Snake to mimic the appearance/texture of any surface he touched. It also has the distinct honor of earning a rare 10/10 review score from Game Informer. Now, thanks to the Metal Gear Solid: Master Collection Vol. 2, we can finally revisit MGS 4 without dusting off a PlayStation 3.

Join recent Metal Gear convert Charles Harte, who will be on the sticks to experience Guns of the Patriots (via the Master Collection Vol. 2) for the very first time, alongside long-time series fan Marcus Stewart, who is revisiting MGS 4 for the first time in over a decade. #4211. Battlefield 6 Season 2 delayed like many of us expected, but we're getting a new update and a bonus battle pass path

Battlefield 6 has pushed back its next season by nearly a month in order to refine Season 2 content and implement more of players' feedback.

Battlefield Studios has released its first official communication in 2026. Rather than unveil the second season of Battlefield 6, however, the developer instead announced a delay. The currently ongoing Season 1 was initially meant to end on Tuesday, January 20, hence why the developer had to communicate something this week.

Season 1 will now end on Tuesday, February 17, which is also when Season 2 will kick off. Given the current sentiment around the game, this news isn’t surprising in the least.

In the blog post announcing the delay, BF Studios said that the decision to extend the current season and push back the start of the next one allows for extra time to “further polish and refine” Season 2 content.

The developer did not offer any hints about Season 2, but there’s an incredibly brief teaser trailer featuring a soldier wearing a gas mask emerging from an environment drenched in toxic gas.

Given that Battlefield 6’s battle royale mode Redsec does not utilise the popular encroaching gas mechanic (using an encroaching ring of fire instead), it’s possible that we may be looking at something new in multiplayer akin to Battlefield 1. Of course, this may just be a visual piece that doesn’t reflect the gameplay of Season 2.

Escalating the fight with new threats on the battlefield.Season 2 begins February 17. pic.twitter.com/fGMegJJuTj

What we are getting news of today, however, is the game’s next patch. This extension update is going to arrive next week, on January 20, when Season 1 was supposed to end. It’s bringing new weekly challenges to the game, but its biggest addition is yet another Bonus Path to the battle pass. You can also expect the free daily login rewards to continue, alongside other periods of double XP.

Similar to other Bonus Paths, the new Frostfire Bonus Path can be completed alongside the Season 1 battle pass. You’ll need 110 Bonus Path Points in total if you want to earn everything it has to offer, with each tier requiring 10 points. It is worth noting, however, that Frostfire Points are only earned through weekly challenges, meaning there won’t be any bonus challenges associated with it.

Frostfire includes several new customisation rewards, of course, such as a Weapon Package, soldier skin, XP boosts and the usual run of unlocks.

Though the latest blog post may be devoid of any real details on Season 2, BF Studios confirmed that Battlefield Labs will play a larger role in offering a preview of what’s to come, so it’s entirely possible that the testing initiative will soon open its doors to players with an early look at some of the maps and other content planned for Season 2.

#4210. The Video Games And More You Should Play This Weekend – October 30, 2026

Welcome to Devil's Night, the night before Halloween, where video games are best served scary. After tomorrow night – Halloween proper – no more scary video games allowed. At least not until mid-September, 2027. I'm sorry, I don't make the rules. Below you will find our weekend gaming recommendations (which is actually surprisingly light on scary games – apologies), but before that, here are some of the biggest stories of the week.

Phantom Blade Zero is one of the best action games I’ve ever played, and it’s certainly one of the most impressive to watch. Beijing-based developer S-Game uses China’s Wuxia brand of action (which was actually banned for some time during the 20th Century by the country’s government) to create a stylish, fluid, and hyper-engaging combat system. It will constantly leave you in awe that action combat can look this good. But looks aren’t everything. Fortunately, Phantom Blade Zero delivers on all fronts, with weapon mechanics so detailed that picking up a new blade can feel like unlocking a new character in a fighting game. The story won’t blow your socks off, but it’s certainly engaging and enticing enough to bring you through Phantom Blade Zero’s 40 or so hours of content. If you’re not interested in the “perfect ending,” which is the only satisfactory one in my opinion, you can complete the game in less than 30 hours. S-Game mixes high-octane combat with sprawling and rewarding exploration to create a must-play during this already busy season of games. You can read more of my thoughts in the Game Informer Phantom Blade Zero review, and if you are hopping in this weekend, be sure to check out my list of Phantom Blade Zero tips and tricks I wish I knew before starting it.

If you have any fond memories of IllFonic’s ill-fated Friday the 13th: The Game as I do, you simply must play the studio’s latest, Halloween: The Game. It is essentially Friday the 13th with Michael Myers instead of Jason, but with a decade of lessons learned from the team’s teeth carving in other horror properties and games. You’re either Michael or a citizen; the former wants to kill you and all the NPCs in various suburban maps, while the latter must rescue as many NPCs as possible while staying alive themselves. It’s that classic cat-and-mouse formula IllFonic is the master of, but with all the style, substance, and synths of John Carpenter’s Halloween masterpiece. Plus, Halloween: The Game features IllFonic’s first crack at a single-player campaign, and while it’s largely a tutorial for playing as Michael, if you’re a Halloween mega-fan like me, it’s worth checking out if only to take part in some of the film’s most iconic kills. You can read more of my thoughts in the Game Informer Halloween: The Game review here, and if you’re hopping in this weekend, there’s a new map, additional Halloween-themed cosmetics to unlock, and more waiting for you.

Overwatch is in the midst of its Halloween event, which have always historically been pretty interesting. This year it's Mystery Madness: Graveyard Games. In it, you begin by picking one of three characters in a random role. And then, as the game progresses, you choose perks that upgrade, alter, or completely change what your character can do. It can get really chaotic where by round three characters like Orisa might be three times her normal size or Torbjorn might have placed a giant turret on Mercy's making her a flying death machine. There are also Halloween skins, as well.

Tom the Postgirl is an odd little adventure that I'd recommend to fans of Untitled Goose Game. You play as Tom, a creepy girl who's tasked with delivering packages to the people of her wacky town, which is depicted with storybook-style illustrations and a color palette limited to black, white, and red. On the surface, you're delivering packages, but the game's real story is based on Tom's tendency to peep where she shouldn't, peering into townsfolks' windows to watch their odd lives. On house is full of kids who live like dogs; another has a couple with a bizarre obsession with tickling. You never know what each window might reveal, and I quickly sympathized with (and enabled) Tom's compulsion. You also have the capacity to cause quite a bit of trouble by stomping on flowers, haphazardly snipping strings and cords, or even stealing packages and using them for your own mischievous purposes. It's a pretty short experience, completable in just a few hours, making it a nice palate cleanser between the massive releases at the end of the year.

This Devolver Digital-published game has a simple but head-turning premise. You’re a profoundly angry woman who returns to her small hometown armed with nothing but a sledgehammer, which she uses to smash everything in sight. The town is also inhabited by robots possessing human consciousnesses. Swinging the hammer can either punch holes through walls or, with enough force, reduce entire buildings to rubble. But why is she doing this? Why is she so mad? A big part of Virtue and a Sledgehammer’s allure is its fascinating and well-written tale about the protagonist’s strained relationships with her sister and mother. Learning more about their lives requires you to keep smashing, but the more you learn, the more you begin to question whether smashing everything is actually a good idea.

This bizarre indie blends fun match-3 puzzle-solving with tower defense gameplay wrapped around a funny but surreal story. The match-3 gameplay involves sliding tiles to match geographic elements like castles, trees, and rivers to collect resources that feed into the tower defense portion. Depending on how the board looks when the puzzle portion ends, you send troops (sustained by the resources you collected) to attack/defend against rival castles and gather more items; board positioning determines how well this can go. The two mechanics feed into each other to create a fun loop that grows in complexity as new mechanics are introduced. Did I mention the game is also very weird? The silly tale centers on a medieval court designating you the chosen savior to rescue their lost queen (and many other tasks), and the dumb tone adds personality to a sometimes dry genre. Titanium Court charmed and impressed us when it launched on PC earlier this year, and now console and mobile players get their chance to hold court.

Sword of the Sea is a beautiful, 2025 game about surfing through the sand atop a floating sword. It recalls Journey, the emotional 2012 PlayStation game, which makes sense as it comes from the artists and developers that worked on that game, developer Giant Squid. Giant Squid also made 2016's Abzû and 2020's The Pathless. It's a talented team and Sword of the Sea maintains that reputation. And now you can play it on Switch 2. You can read my full review of the game (though this review pertains to the PlayStation 5 version) right here.

Cities: Skylines arrived on PC more than a decade ago, but is still revered as one of the greatest modern city-builders. Even now, three years after the sequel's release, Paradox continues supporting and porting the original game. A couple years after its initial release, Cities: Skylines received a strong console port, which did an admirable job of adapting the controls to gamepads, but the Switch version was always the weakest of the bunch. As of this week, Switch 2 owners can play a less compromised version, expanding the Switch's 9-tile limit to a much larger 25-tile limit, as well as better performance and textures, better control panels, and a ton of DLC and added content. And on top of that, if you own the Switch 1 version, you get a deep discount on the Switch 2 version.

While not specifically about this new Switch 2 version, you can read our original reviews of the base PC version here, and the base console version here.

Minecraft has held its dominant spot in pop culture for so long that it's easy to forget a simple fact about it: the game is awesome. This week, it's coming to Switch 2, giving potential miners another platform to explore procedurally-generated caves in. You've certainly heard of it, and you've probably played it, but I still feel it often doesn't get the flowers it deserves in high-level critical discussions about games, despite its regular cadence of major updates. The opening gameplay loop is so satisfying that for many of my peers, whether they regularly play video games or not, it's only a matter of time before they boot up a new world again. While you can never play the game for the first time again, if you haven't checked it out in a couple years, you might be surprised by the amount of new blocks, materials, and mobs they've added in recent updates. And if you've never played before, the Switch 2 launch is as good a time as any to see what all the fuss is about.

The card game incarnation of Arkham Horror remains one of the best narrative-driven and horror-themed tabletop games around, and it's an easy recommendation if you're looking for something engaging to dive into on Halloween night. Rooted in the monsters and mysteries of the Cthulhu Mythos, this living card game is built on major core sets and expansions. But unlike a TCG, each new installment has the same cards included, fueling the cooperative adventures you'll undertake together with your fellow players. Last year Arkham Horror: The Card Game did something of a soft relaunch for a chapter 2 of its narrative, and that new core set is an ideal place to jump on  play. Players each control an individual investigator as they explore arcane and weird mysteries, confront monsters, and unfold plots of cultists, ancient entities, and forbidden lore. For fans of cosmic horror storytelling, it's an easy pick.
